Researchers who read the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, especially its philosophical heritage, through historical questions in this general sense all belong somewhere along this line.
Among them are also those whose work goes beyond a general historical approach and adopts a specifically scientific method based on the principles of historical materialism.

These, then, are four intellectual approaches that have shaped many attempts, in different periods, to understand what medieval Arab-Islamic thinkers produced in fields such as theology, jurisprudence, law, philosophy, the natural and mathematical sciences, literature, and others.
We do not claim that these four approaches are the only ones that have shaped such studies. There are countless other ways in which people have approached this heritage.
But we can say that the first three, despite their differences in style, all grow out of one general intellectual method: an ahistorical method.
What ultimately unites them is the idealist position.
From that same position come other ways of looking at intellectual production, and from it also comes the broader ahistorical method that provides the general framework for approaches of this kind.
We have used the methodological classification as the main basis for our survey of how historians and researchers have approached our intellectual heritage.

But this does not mean that we can dispense with the descriptive classification. That second classification helps us place each position within its own historical, intellectual, and ideological setting.
As we have already said, it divides historians and researchers into three broad groups: ancient writers; modern Arab and Eastern writers; and Orientalists and other Western researchers.
We can now examine the positions found within each group.
To understand how ancient Arab and Eastern writers approached this heritage, we have to go far back in time—back to a period when the heritage had not yet become heritage at all.
It was still the living present.

It was still being born and continually renewed. It was growing and changing. People devoted themselves to it, argued over it, and developed their own specialties within it. It raised problems for them, and they in turn raised new problems within it.
Different positions toward it already existed at that stage, before it had become a heritage inherited from the past.
Once it did become a heritage, new positions continued to appear in both East and West. They still appear today, and they will continue to appear in the future.

During the period when this body of thought was first developing, it moved through several stages: from purely Islamic theological forms, to theological-rational forms in Muʿtazilite kalām, then to its first philosophical form with al-Kindī, and finally to mature forms of philosophy that became independent in content from theological thought, beginning with al-Fārābī.
At every stage, this developing intellectual tradition provoked debate and was itself provoked by debate. It entered into conflicts and became the target of conflict.
It was always “partisan” in one sense or another, and it was always challenged by opposing forms of partisanship.

In every period it became the subject of disagreement and controversy. These intellectual and ideological struggles reflected, to different degrees, the social and political struggles taking place at each stage in the history of Arab-Islamic society.

The question of divine decree and human freedom was the first major issue that Arab-Islamic thought approached in a rational and explicitly “partisan” way—that is, from a defined intellectual position and with a political starting point, namely opposition to Umayyad rule.

As this question became one of the central intellectual issues debated between the first and second centuries AH, beginning around the middle of the seventh century, supporters and opponents entered into an increasingly intense struggle.
Those who opposed the rejection of predestination used religious authority to intimidate the other side.
Al-Muṣʿab al-Zubayrī, for example, reports Mālik ibn Anas (96–179 AH / 714–795 CE) as saying:
“I dislike discussion in religion. The people of our city have always disliked it and forbidden it, such as discussion of Jahm’s views, divine decree, and similar matters...”

The opponents of human freedom went even further. They used religion to distort the position they were attacking by calling its supporters the Qadariyya, even though that name would seem more logically suited to those who believed the opposite—that human acts were determined.
The purpose was to apply to the supporters of free choice a saying attributed to the Prophet:
“The Qadariyya are the Magians of this community.”
The Muʿtazilites rejected the label. They argued:
“The term Qadariyya applies to those who say that divine decree, both good and evil, comes from God.”
And that was not their own position.
The Muʿtazilites then developed the rational tendency further and gave it stronger theoretical foundations, drawing on philosophical influences from several sources.
Their movement marked a turning point in Arab-Islamic thought in two important areas.
The Muʿtazilites broke with the idea that knowledge could have only one source, namely divine revelation. They added reason as another source of knowledge, even in questions of religious belief.
The second concerned human freedom and responsibility.
They built their understanding of divine justice on the idea that human beings are free and therefore responsible for their own actions. In doing so, they rejected absolute determinism.
Opposition soon developed against both sides of this position.
Religion was again used as a tool to restrain Muʿtazilite rationalism and to block its possible development toward a philosophical form of thought more independent of theology.
During the period when Muʿtazilism was at its height, this opposition was represented by three main currents: the Salafi current, the Hanbali current, and the Ashʿarī current.
All three shared one basic feature: hostility toward the relatively progressive elements in Muʿtazilite thought.
• By the middle of the ninth century CE, the conservative currents had combined their efforts to remove Muʿtazilite thought almost completely from active intellectual life.
The disappearance of the Muʿtazilites from the intellectual scene was followed by the almost complete disappearance of their original writings from Arab-Islamic libraries.
As a result, later generations were left with Muʿtazilite ideas mainly as their opponents had presented them: scattered, shortened, and removed from their original context.
Later readers were therefore denied the chance to encounter Muʿtazilite thought in the complete form in which the Muʿtazilites themselves had written it.
Only a very small number of their original works eventually reached us.

These included al-Intiṣār by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Khayyāṭ, along with several manuscripts discovered in Yemen by an Egyptian scholarly mission in relatively recent years. Some volumes of one of these works, al-Mughnī by the Muʿtazilite judge ʿAbd al-Jabbār, were later published in Egypt.

It is clear to us now that this hostility would not have reached the point of almost erasing the Muʿtazilite heritage if its real target had not been the strong tendency toward intellectual freedom that ran through that heritage.

The campaign against Muʿtazilite thought continued into later periods and eventually took the form of hostility toward other kinds of thought based on reason, including the natural sciences, philosophy, and mathematics.
• Al-Masʿūdī describes how conservative Sunnis viewed Muʿtazilite thought under the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil.

He writes that although al-Mutawakkil was “one of the most unjust caliphs,” the Sunni scholars praised him and overlooked his actions because he had ended the miḥna—by which al-Masʿūdī means the period in which Muʿtazilite doctrine had official power. He adds that many hadith scholars claimed to have seen al-Mutawakkil in dreams in which they were told that God had forgiven him.
Al-Suyūṭī gives us a similar example from the jurists and hadith scholars.

He tells us that during al-Mutawakkil’s reign, Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba sat in the Ruṣāfa Mosque while his brother sat in the Manṣūr Mosque, and both encouraged the people to pray for al-Mutawakkil and praise him.
But opposition went much further than praise for al-Mutawakkil.
Muʿtazilite thought was attacked, distorted, and sometimes deliberately misrepresented.
Al-Isfarāyīnī, for example, gave a remarkable interpretation of Muʿtazilite texts on divine justice.
The Muʿtazilites had argued that human power is limited by the power of God.
Al-Isfarāyīnī, one of the major Ashʿarī writers, interpreted their position in an extraordinary way.
Because the Muʿtazilites held that human beings create their own acts, he claimed that their view meant:

“Every one of them—even the gnat, the mosquito, the bee, the ant, and the worm—is a creator, creating its own acts. God is not the creator of their acts and has no power over any of them. Indeed, He has no power over anything done by all the animals. They therefore establish countless creators (...) and in doing so prepare the way for dualism.”
This interpretation ignores the fact that when Muʿtazilite texts speak of “God’s servants” in this context, they mean human beings.

It also ignores the fact that the Muʿtazilites could hardly be accused of dualism. They defended the absolute unity of God so strongly that they fought bitter intellectual battles against dualists, as well as against those who gave God human-like qualities or a bodily form.

• Ibn Khaldūn may have been the only major ancient writer who, despite his own Ashʿarī allegiance, understood the importance of the historical conditions that made Muʿtazilite thought so attractive to many people of its time.
He recognized that the Muʿtazilite period was also a period of scientific development.

In his view, this historical reality helped philosophy spread and made people increasingly interested in it. It also created the conditions in which the Muʿtazilites could introduce what he called their “innovation”—a word that reflects his own Ashʿarī standpoint.
The Muʿtazilites used philosophy in their arguments, Ibn Khaldūn explains, and this made it difficult for their opponents to refute them because their arguments rested on philosophical foundations.
He then says that this was precisely why Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī took on the task of defending Sunni doctrine through rational arguments—in other words, by using the Muʿtazilites’ own weapon.

Later Ashʿarī thinkers followed the same path. They introduced logic into their discussions and eventually philosophy as well, while still keeping the questions of kalām separate from the questions of philosophy.
Ibn Khaldūn points in particular to the works of al-Ghazālī and “Imam Ibn al-Khaṭīb” as models of this approach.
He criticizes later theologians for confusing the two methods: the method of Sunni kalām and the method of the philosophers.
Whatever Ibn Khaldūn himself intended, his discussion amounts to an indirect admission that the Muʿtazilites were the first to make the relationship between kalām and philosophy a historical reality.
Among the ancient Arab-Islamic thinkers, Ibn Khaldūn stands out for his sharp historical sense.

It gave his interpretation of events a more scientific character and allowed him to look beyond surface appearances, even though he remained an opponent of the Muʿtazilites because of his Ashʿarī commitments.
In fact, it is fair to say that his allegiance did not prevent him from seeing the deeper connection between the development of the sciences and the development of philosophical thought.

He understood that this connection helped explain the success of the Muʿtazilites. He also understood that the same historical conditions later allowed Ashʿarī kalām to become one of the two major successors to Muʿtazilite theology.
The other successor was philosophy itself.
The struggle had originally been between two main intellectual currents.
The first, represented by the Muʿtazilites, was trying to free itself from its theological ties, although it never fully succeeded.

The second insisted that thought must remain tied to theology. The Ashʿarī school eventually became the most advanced form of this second current because it was less isolated from the wider intellectual development of its time.
The historical forces behind this conflict were too powerful for the suppression of Muʿtazilite thought to end the conflict itself.
Those forces followed objective laws. They did not depend on personal wishes or deliberate decisions.
So even though Muʿtazilite thought was removed by force, the struggle did not disappear.
Instead, it moved into a higher form.
After the Muʿtazilites themselves vanished from the scene, the conflict developed along two major paths that remained in tension with one another until what we call the modern period.
The first path was philosophy: what we call Arab-Islamic philosophy.
This new division marked a qualitative change in the form of the struggle.
The earlier conflict had been between pure theology and a form of theology that had become rationalized.
